expected.longDescription:
Project Quarm is a community EverQuest server that uses the TAKP classic client and login system. It runs the classic ruleset with its own progression and quality-of-life changes. PlayBound can install the public client for you, but you create your account through the project's own site.

It is an unofficial community project and is not run by Daybreak.

set.longDescription:
Project Quarm is EverQuest for people who want the old world but have one character's worth of time. It is a fan-run, free emulated server built around one rule: one box. Each player runs one character, with no army of alternate accounts following them around, which pushes everybody back toward the thing the game was always about: finding a group.

The server progresses through the eras in order, from classic through Kunark, Velious and Luclin, with the 2002 Planes of Power expansion as the planned final stop. So your character can grow with the world instead of arriving after everything is finished. Check the community guide to see where it currently stands, since the timeline moves along.

It is not a pure museum piece. The team has added shared banks, automatic corpse dragging and chat channels, and some players feel it has moved toward being a custom server. In practice, those changes remove old annoyances while keeping the slow, social rhythm intact, though purists may prefer Project 1999, listed here too. Quarm suits anyone who wants the later classic expansions and fair competition for camps. It draws on the TAKProject and Al'Kabor codebases and is free and open source.

expected.longDescription:
HorizonXI is a volunteer-run Final Fantasy XI server, live since 17 December 2022 and built on the AirSkyBoat codebase. It recreates the game as it played in its earlier years, with a progression that unlocks content over time, and it currently reaches Treasures of Aht Urhgan with a level cap of 75.

It is an unofficial private server and requires your own copy of the game data.

set.longDescription:
HorizonXI asks what Final Fantasy XI would have become if the level cap had never been raised above 75. It is a free private server launched in December 2022, built on the Chains of Promathia era, and it describes itself as "era+": a return to that period with custom balancing, rather than a strict recreation.

That means you get the older, slower game, with long roads between cities, real danger outside the walls and a party-based climb that takes a very long time. Reaching the level cap is a serious undertaking, and most people will spend many months getting there. Horizon adjusts things along the way, including small changes such as lowering the level for Auto Refresh, and its wiki keeps a list of the public changes. Some of the era+ code remains deliberately private, so not every detail is documented, and players do argue about choices like the level sync experience penalty.

Above all, it offers a big and active community, which is the thing an old MMO needs most, and that is what makes grouping possible again. It is a good choice for lapsed players who miss Vana'diel as it was. It is not official, and the client is set up through the server's own instructions.

expected.longDescription: SWG Legends focuses on the New Game Experience era. Get the client from their official download page only.

set.longDescription:
SWG Legends keeps the later version of Star Wars Galaxies alive. Where most emulator servers chase the game's early Pre-CU era, this one is built around the NGE ruleset, the version that followed the game's controversial 2005 overhaul, and it modifies that ruleset to its own taste. It has long been one of the larger NGE communities.

That choice shapes what you play. Combat is more direct and action-oriented, Jedi is available from the start of your character's life rather than being a distant unlock, and the galaxy is open for players who simply want to be a Star Wars hero without spending months on the road to get there. It is also a real sandbox still, with player cities, crafting and a community that likes to build and role-play in it.

So the choice between servers really comes down to which Galaxies you loved. If you want the old skill-tree game, Infinity, also listed here, is the better fit. If you remember the NGE fondly or just want more immediate action, Legends should feel right at home. It is a free, fan-run server with no connection to Sony or Lucasfilm. The rules and systems change as its team develops them, so check the community's pages for what is current.

expected.longDescription: Ashes 2063 is Vostyok's post-apocalyptic GZDoom campaign set in the south-eastern United States. Its maps lean on classic Build-engine design: tight interiors, secrets and scavenged weapons, with a lonely roads atmosphere influenced by Fallout. This edition includes the Afterglow follow-up content.

set.longDescription:
Ashes 2063 is the Doom mod that barely looks like Doom any more. Vostyok's total conversion for GZDoom replaces virtually everything in the original game to tell a tongue-in-cheek post-apocalyptic story inspired by Mad Max, Fallout, S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and Metro 2033. Released in 2018 with ten levels, and a Cacowards runner-up, it plays more like a lost 1990s shooter than like a mod.

You ride a motorbike through a ruined world, scavenging for ammunition and fighting raiders and mutants. There is a new arsenal with a proper reloading system, along with new power-ups and enemies that have more advanced AI than Doom's marching demons. Levels feel like real places, with garages, wasteland towns and flooded tunnels instead of abstract techbases, and they are full of secrets and little jokes for anyone who explores.

Reviewers often compare it to Duke Nukem 3D and Blood, and that gets the tone about right: gritty, funny and very pleased with itself. The series grew later with the Dead Man Walking expansion and a second episode, Afterglow. This edition runs on GZDoom with Freedoom underneath, so nothing needs buying. If you try only one Doom total conversion, this is a good one to choose. It rewards a slower pace than Doom itself does.

expected.longDescription: Pirate Doom! rebuilds Doom II as a Caribbean raid. Every stock monster gets a pirate treatment, from peg-leg zombies to cannon-armed bosses, with new weapons, music and maps. It runs on GZDoom and is a good example of how far a Doom total conversion can go.

set.longDescription:
Pirate Doom asks a question nobody else had thought to ask: what if Doom were also The Secret of Monkey Island? This total conversion by Arch, built for GZDoom, stars an unnamed heroic captain who is up against LeChuck himself, and it reworks almost all of Doom II into a bright, cartoon pirate adventure that is much funnier than a game about shooting things has any right to be.

Every monster from Doom II gets a complete visual and audio redesign to fit the theme, so you are blasting undead sailors rather than imps. The weapons are overhauled as well, including a gatling gun that needs time to spin up before unleashing a high rate of fire. Dozens of levels take you from coves and pirate villages to a circus and eventually hell itself, so it keeps surprising you well after the joke might have worn off.

Underneath the costume, it keeps Doom's simple pleasures, which is what makes it work. Reviewers praised how well it captures those charms rather than just decorating them. It runs here on GZDoom with Freedoom underneath, so no purchase of Doom is needed. If you enjoy it, there is a much larger sequel out there, Pirate Doom 2. Bring friends if you can, and shout at them in pirate voices.

expected.longDescription: PlayBound copies your legitimate GOG installation of Ground Control II and layers the community Essentials pack over the copy, leaving your original install untouched. The pack fixes launch problems on modern Windows and adds quality-of-life changes for current hardware.

set.longDescription:
This edition is Ground Control 2: Operation Exodus made to work the way it should in 2026. It combines the original 2004 real-time tactics game with GC2: Essentials, an unofficial all-in-one pack of community fixes, so you do not have to hunt around old forums to get a smooth installation. It supports version 1.0.0.8 of the game from Steam or GOG, and you still need your own copy.

The fixes target the things that stop you from enjoying the game at all. Some wireless devices used to prevent it from launching, and that is resolved. The camera zoom is improved, which matters a lot in a game about reading terrain, and a 16:9 fix corrects the aspect ratio of most interface elements so that they render properly on a modern monitor.

The most important change may be multiplayer. The original GameSpy servers are long gone, so the pack points the game at community-run OpenSpy servers and restores online play. That brings back the game's battles, where you buy reinforcements in the field and capture points to earn more, instead of the usual business of building a base. The pack is unaffiliated with Massive Entertainment or Vivendi, and it was first released in January 2026. It suits both returning commanders and curious newcomers.

expected.longDescription: The PlayBound way to play Heroes III with friends. The HD Mod leaves the original campaigns and balance intact while adding modern resolutions, widescreen support, a better interface and improved online and hot-seat play. PlayBound handles installing it over your Heroes III Complete copy.

set.longDescription:
This edition is the practical way to play Heroes of Might and Magic III on a modern PC, particularly with other people. It is built around baratorch's fan-made HD Mod, a long-standing add-on that does not touch the original game files. Rather than remaking the game, it removes what has aged badly, starting with resolution. The 1999 game runs at high resolutions, including ultrawide, so far more of the adventure map fits on the screen.

The online side is what gives this edition its name. The HD Mod includes an online lobby, which makes it easy to find a game with friends without the old networking trouble. It is also designed to work closely with Horn of the Abyss, which has a dedicated lobby of its own, so the two together are what much of the community uses to play today.

It does not change the rules or balance of the game itself, which is the point. Your castles, heroes and creature stacks all behave as you remember, and those long turns of a Heroes match are still there to enjoy over an evening. You need your own copy of Heroes III Complete or The Shadow of Death. Note that this is not Ubisoft's official HD Edition on Steam, which is a separate product.

expected.longDescription: A fan-created expansion that revitalises Star Wars: Galactic Battlegrounds for modern systems, adding factions, units and fixes.

set.longDescription:
Expanding Fronts is the massive community expansion that Star Wars Galactic Battlegrounds never got from LucasArts. It builds on a game already powered by the Age of Empires II engine, and it sets out to make each of the original civilizations feel more unique and true to the setting, while adding new playable ones in later versions. Version 1.5.0, its largest update, added three new civilizations.

The amount of content here is staggering. Hundreds of new units, buildings, props and effects draw on the wider Star Wars universe, including Expanded Universe and newer Clone Wars material, so you will see a lot of ships and troopers the 2001 game never had. There are new terrains and larger map sizes too. For scenario makers, the editor gains all that content plus new trigger conditions and effects, which gives campaign designers far more freedom.

Newer campaigns extend the story side as well, including one set in the Episode I era and a Battle of Jakku campaign, and there is a co-op campaign add-on. Widescreen support and a higher frame rate also help the old game fit modern screens. If you have ever wanted your Galactic Battlegrounds matches to feel bigger, this is the way to do it. You need your own copy of the Saga edition.

expected.longDescription: UCP3 fixes long-standing problems in Stronghold Crusader, opens it to modular balance sets, and supports custom AI. This edition is packaged for easy installation.

set.longDescription:
The Unofficial Crusader Patch is what the Stronghold Crusader community has used for years to keep improving Firefly's 2002 classic, and version 3 turns it from a single patch into a whole framework. It covers bug fixes, unit rebalancing and quality-of-life changes, along with new content such as maps and AI lords. It contains no Firefly files, so it needs your own copy of the game, and it only officially supports versions 1.41 and 1.41.1 in Latin-language releases.

The new design is what sets version 3 apart. Modules change the game's code and add features, while plugins carry content and configurations like maps, AI and gameplay setups. You choose what is active in a list, with higher entries overriding lower ones, so your game can be as close to the original or as heavily changed as you like. AI extensions are the most popular part, because new lords are one of the best ways to get more out of a game people already know by heart.

PlayBound's edition handles the setup that would otherwise take a few steps, so you can get straight to your castle. It is open source under the GPL version 3. There is no UCP for the Definitive Edition at the moment, so this is for Crusader HD only.

expected.longDescription: TrueCombat: Elite is a long-running Enemy Territory conversion that swaps class-based fantasy for a military simulation.

set.longDescription:
TrueCombat:Elite takes Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, one of the great free team shooters, and turns it into something much slower and much more dangerous. It is a free total conversion set in modern urban warfare, built around realism and tactics, and its heart lies in how quickly a mistake ends your round.

The biggest change is how you aim. There is no crosshair, so you rely on iron sights and real weapon behaviour instead of a dot in the middle of your screen. Two teams have 16 weapons each, 32 in total, with heavier roles such as snipers paying for it in mobility. Rounds become careful exercises in checking corners and listening, and a sudden firefight is over within seconds. It was a real influence on players who wanted more than arcade shooting at the time, and it is still a distinctive way to play Enemy Territory's engine.

Be realistic about its age, though. Most of what is written about it dates from 2005 to 2011, and it is no longer in active development, so expect to bring your own friends rather than finding busy servers. That makes it a good party choice for a tense evening. It runs on top of Enemy Territory 2.60b, which PlayBound's install takes care of.
